Due to the petition between both their fan bases, Thomas Pynchon and Chuck Tingle collaborate on a Chuck Tingle-sized novel. Tingle-sized content for the buckaroos and lady buckaroos, and a window into the buried histories of the post-modern world for the Pynchinites. The two authors start with a title, and the book grows from the title: Dr. Knubble And The Fangs Of The Love Sharks.

dataFragment.data:
Dr. Knubble & His Bellyfloss
A Novel by
Chuck Tingle
It starts with my first ever encounter with love, I mean actual human romantic love between women. I was eight at the time, and my father took me on a trip out west with his family to meet my grandmother who had come all the way from Canada. This meeting, the granddaddy-busting reunion that it proved to be, would prove a defining moment not just in my childhood life, but for many other people too, and it all came down to my cousin Milly and her best friend Amy—I
. . . now it is your turn, Mr. Pynchon!

Okay fine whatever, we get it: Miley and Amy. But please don't call them that, I'm still angry about it (even if Miley did say she wasn't really pissed off anymore). In any case, it was these two friends of mine, plus their mother Gretta—who'd brought over some maple syrup she made herself from her sugar tree out in the yard back home in Quebec province—who decided to throw a party to show my father and me our great auntie Nana's beautiful face after having passed us around so much over the years without even knowing who we were, but now

suddenly here we were standing right in front of her smiling, talking to us, hugging and touching. So what could've possibly happened after that, Mr. T? Well like I said earlier, it was my father and me that found ourselves falling deeply head over heels for one of those beautiful creatures from across the sea—but then the whole thing changed for me. It changed because Milly and Gretta began showing an almost maternal interest in me—they gave me presents; things they thought might catch the eye and interest me—and their affection for me turned into genuine caring for me in a way that neither my father

or I have known since—so maybe the most surprising aspect of this tale is how the rest of our journey back home was actually quite peaceful as far as my emotions went, until the very end, when something horrible, unspeakably horrible indeed occurred. Something, I believe, that changed me irrevocably forever and led me onto the road to self discovery which would eventually take me all the way to this book—that of course, being this book—and that is the story you will hear below. Or at least, you would, had the publisher allowed us to write this chapter in the style of the great H

. Pym, and included footnotes throughout, instead of letting you experience this entire journey through our writing the story as we see fit. Oh sure the author can explain everything and tell you where you're going wrong and why, but really there's nothing more frustrating and infuriating than to have someone else tell you the obvious and then fail to acknowledge their own faults—which, if anything, only makes the person who has the fault feel more stupid and foolish for their error, whereas when you yourself are told, oh you know you got it completely backward, the knowledge helps make you look less silly, and thus you begin

:
Chapter 1:

Dr. Knubble And The Bellyflops
I never realized before just how funny and weird it must've been, the way you could be sitting in a car driving down a highway at a high rate of speed and then stop for a second, maybe go twenty feet and do another three or four seconds of accelerating and stop again, then do another ten or fifteen seconds of acceleration and finally pull over to park the car, the person getting into the driver’s seat looking straight ahead at the passing scenery with a sort of intense expression, their arms hanging out of the open window, and the person in the

passenger seat who’d been sitting next to them just watching out the window while saying, I wonder how fast this vehicle would be going if we kept driving it at this pace?
I had this same sort of expression on my face the first time, only that’s exactly the moment I met Dr. Robert A. "Bob" Knubble.
Dr. Knubble and Miley Cyrus
A novel by:
Thomas Pynchon & Chuck Tingle
This all took place a couple weeks later, and my first impression was this.

Wow I think to myself, the only reason we even bothered to stop here is so I could see a man in an orange suit. But then he looks at me in that calm and relaxed fashion he has, the smile coming over him and his whole body shaking slightly, causing a soft vibration that’s not too hard and yet not quite enough to send a thrill up and down your spinal column either—he smiles like he knows something special is about to happen, and I am so struck by the feeling, which seems both sweet and powerful at the same time, that the sight and his manner, plus the smell of

that fresh-sanded woodsy aroma I always find so relaxing and uplifting, causes me somehow to surrender to this overwhelming emotion of a deep desire to just relax and be with him—it feels as if the universe has given us permission, and I don't even want to know why—this was the exact moment when I decided that my whole purpose in life now consisted not of trying to become a great artist, nor of becoming famous and respected for having created something important—instead I now wished only for an ordinary life where the most beautiful and precious things would appear to be what they actually were, that is: totally

unexpected events—in short, all the good stuff that can happen between two strangers on a road trip with a mother who brought them maple syrup.
I was thinking about this whole situation as I walked around inside Dr. Knubble's office and checked the appointment books—all filled to capacity, with many new patients in for consultations already waiting their turn—while the old doctor was in one of the back rooms examining and giving advice and guidance to some lucky and wealthy client. I didn't really understand all the terms being used and heard the words 'brevoxen', 'bifidophorus', and even

a little bit of 'cretacean', but that just meant 'like the crabs', so in essence what this all came down to, in the simplest of simple terms—the only terms the people around me needed to grasp at that moment—was I knew for certain now, after my own recent personal transformation into something more and better than before, I now felt more than ready to join Dr. Knubble in helping him give other poor souls the very special chance of finding their own bliss. That’s why it was me and my mother—and the maple syrup that Gretta carried around with her

like a purse or pocketbook or whatever you call it that we brought back from Canada with her—who decided it was best for me to accompany her on our way back east when the three-day family vacation was over, and I remember my mother asking if she could stay a week in New Jersey or Pennsylvania somewhere so she wouldn't have any excuses if Milly got pregnant while we still lived there—as I recall, this idea was shot down by Amy immediately, saying she'd never be able to forgive Milly or herself.

Then Milly, being who she was and always trying to keep a handle of control over all the situations and people and things in the world and the cosmos and the planet and everything that happens in it and on it, said if you and your sister can get along without you, I certainly won’t be holding my breath and waiting until the baby is born before the whole damn thing starts going off and exploding again.

And that of course set us up for our roadtrip, though I wasn't to learn of this right away, because the truth about why I ended up in that particular location on the road—and it would have seemed completely random if it weren't for all those years my father spent studying and learning how everything worked and how it all fit together; he taught me a lot—is I guess you could call it the ultimate accident, but really just part of the natural order of the universe.

Okay well first off, the car my father drove was the old green Honda Civic. He and my mom always had that car in perfect condition, no matter what kind of terrible mess it looked and sounded in, and whenever we needed money to go anywhere or do anything or take a break and go to the mall or something to eat, it just miraculously appeared out of thin air, usually within twenty-four hours—not even thirty-six! My mother, bless her soul, believed the world was run and ordered by forces far greater than any individual person, so when I once asked her how she did something so
--here Pynchon falls asleep, and Chuck Tingle takes over the narrative for the duration of Pynchon's sleepytime:

I believe in a great big world where everyone gets along. Like we always talk about in school and everybody wants everybody else’s business to succeed, and all that. Well I believe that sometimes the whole plan goes out the window, even with my dad driving the car like I am, which is why I feel we should make a quick exit and start heading north to a nearby motel, but I know we must stick to our current route or the universe might send someone who can tell what’s happened, so I ask myself how could that happen?

And the answer comes as if it is written on a blackboard: We would have made a sudden turn into that parking space—there, by the bank—to stop to use one of their bathrooms and maybe buy a magazine—I forget which magazine—that would be where the whole problem occurred.
So then we come upon that empty space that was just waiting to receive my dear friend Chuck, and when I pull up to the spot next—” ‘To be continued’ the voice behind my left shoulder whispers into the ear that is always closest to him—the moment my eyes are open and the door

shuts itself and the seat moves down to reveal the sweetest most wonderful ass I've ever laid eyes on in all of human existence—which of course I'm only too happy to discover—a man walks up, he says hi to both me and my father in that very friendly manner people often adopt when trying not to appear suspicious and creepy. But since I'm a pretty smart guy I can easily pick up on his feelings about all this and it becomes obvious what is really bothering him: This is a place for married people and families, so how dare a guy like me be coming in there and sitting with them, as

if there wasn't some rule against doing that? It's almost comical how I immediately become embarrassed, and I don't know what the rules say in terms of being able to park right here without anyone getting mad, or being charged for this spot, but anyway it feels like a whole lot more is at stake here, and it is only when my dad looks around the car and asks if we shouldn't drive off right now before things go from bad to worse—because this isn't exactly what you’d call normal, right?

That's why the two men get all tense. I mean my mother has gone back to sleep after having the dream again and my father and I, the poor sap that just had a dream that is now making me even less inclined to want to be near him anymore, have no idea that there are actually people living in that building across from us, with families, with lives of their own. So I try really hard to remain calm while telling myself that this could be any ordinary motel, but instead of saying that I also think the world might actually come crashing down and destroy itself in a fiery blaze if that happens—which

is the only real reason why it doesn't—instead, I say:
“What? Did I hear my name called out there? I’m sorry. You just said, did I hear your name called out there? Yes you certainly heard my friend calling me Chuckie over here, but you need to watch out for that—some folks who work at a lot of motels around the area and other places like this will try very hard to pretend they didn't notice a young couple walking up and sitting right down there

beside them and all that stuff. I guess you should have been paying closer attention to who you’re talking with and whether or not there's someone who works at the motel sitting over there listening in to every word, so of course he can’t help but notice when my mom wakes up screaming—that would definitely make sense if she had done it a hundred times in front of people—and that makes my daddy realize that we really ought to be heading off somewhere before someone calls an ambulance for the rest of you.
Both Tingle and Pynchon are awake and dawdling over chapter 2. You can see their literary scuffles in (parenthesis):

“And the whole thing about why he decided to call himself 'Thomas P. Sample,' which I think it's a little weird and strange to start off the book that way, you have to know how much time and effort it took my old man to research that kind of crap. All kinds of things had happened in the history of this town, which meant it made him a big believer and advocate of researching anything and everything, no matter how seemingly useless and stupid it seemed, so naturally when we got out there it wasn't too difficult to find somebody who'd worked at the place before and who was still living
Chapter 2: There Lies the Knubbins

!
 A small child runs up the sidewalk. The child looks like it belongs in the circus. I wonder if I can run up the same way—I try it—my foot catches on the uneven sidewalk. I slip on the loose asphalt and slide backwards, bumping my head painfully. Then another one pops up. This kid is running towards the parking lot and is wearing shorts so long I have to keep a constant lookout for them, which causes the whole time-lag problem that I’ve mentioned, but this time it doesn’t matter because by the time I catch sight of the kid

my friend Chuck Tingle’s already got him! He's got his hands wrapped tightly in a large towel that he holds in front of him. Tingle stops short.
The two children are running together and yelling excitedly, and it sounds like “Mommy”. They both jump over a hedge, but the older boy loses his balance and lands in a crouched position with a heavy splash, but Tingle catches the younger child before he gets up. I run to them and look over the little guy’s head to see his mother, a thin woman who is holding her hands to

her cheeks as if in shock and staring up with big wide eyes into Tingle’s face. She is dressed very formally—black shoes, gray slacks and a white silk shirt—and I notice for the first time that her hair has begun to gray. As I approach her I notice a slight smell in the air. The scent of decay seems stronger today, like it might even have some faint hint of sulfur or hydrogen sulfide about it...I know I’ve never noticed this before and maybe that means the situation is only getting stranger and scarier?
(Let us make this Black Mirror scary. Existential sci fi dread, whaddya say Pynch?)

Anyway as the mother and I approach she begins talking in a slow monotone, the voice almost dead: “We just moved in, and we don’t know any neighbors—it’s all brand new construction, no one’s around—we haven’t met anyone yet, and this isn’t a good place for kids. This neighborhood isn’t good for kids at all. What is that man doing? We’re in our bathtub—I don’t want the water to go all dirty and stinky, you know what a tub is
(how about a lab where all viruses are birthed from a scientific penis.)

I can’t let the little guy run out into traffic, there might be an accident. This is a bad, unsafe place for children. I just wanted a fresh start in a nice new place and everything, I’m sorry if we disturbed you but this area is too dangerous for my son. He should be home with me—he’s only three and a half, I’ll give you my number, I’m sorry we intruded. I don’t want to bother you anymore.
(But the scientific penis knows no bounds, eh Pynchie?)

You shouldn’t have brought that towel—that thing is bad for him, the germs—no germs, he won’t have to get sick—I hope, I hope—this neighborhood has too many homeless and crazy old ladies and junkies and that is the last place we should be. Please take care, bye. And my apologies, you are free to do with him whatever you want, we can pay—but please call the cops, we were scared—”
Tingle looks at the mother and then takes a long look at the child and then says:
"You
are now in a Pynchon/Tingle joint. We have written you in! Do you have any requests before you take on a life of your own?

Chapter 4, The Biggest Thing of All
The following day—a Monday—after having a nightmare for which my brain is now very tired of remembering the details, it was only because I didn’t want to sleep that I found the strength and determination to wake up, get dressed and come down the hall to check things out, which in the dream had been my father and me walking around this house in some kind of secret location.
Now in real life there are people living here in various places all the time—people with their lives going forward, who would like to be left alone, or at
least unbothered by hootenany.

And I can see where they would need privacy, even if only a temporary reprieve. So what if we don’t know where these other tenants of ours have gone for good. It may not even mean anything that there’s someone living over our heads who is so intent on keeping to himself. But the dream I’d had last night was much too intense and involved to leave things like it—it seemed as if my mind were still looking back into a very different time and space, and in order to understand why it felt so necessary to investigate, I thought I needed some clues about the world
(cue the membrane between the worlds!)

that I was coming out of. Maybe I should find a friend who could read this story and tell me exactly what is meant by it all, a way for us both to better get through it, as the saying goes: the truth, my friend, shall set you right? Or even better than a friend who could interpret: a stranger, maybe someone whose mind has become totally and forever disconnected from the reality we all live in. A completely alien being, an outsider of some sort who would see what I’m trying to show, and then tell me how it’s really meant.

In other words, a psychic or an intuitive! That’s always been the easiest explanation for why so few of us actually ever seem to hear voices, but now that it has been explained for me—in more ways and in more depth than I ever wanted to know about—what are the alternatives, and is it even worth thinking about? Is it worth investigating further and asking about what happened after I’ve gone through the door, if I don’t believe I’ll go inside, because in the future, the real future, I can imagine that the door will open into an even more
orthoganal set of alternate futures. Ones that are not too drastically diffetent than this one.

I guess maybe there won’t be much of a future after I get to it—maybe it’s just like in the dreams where the characters die at the beginning of the movie? What does that say about me?
I am getting confused and I am also starting to worry about whether or not it might help me in the end, or even before that—if I keep putting these two strange ideas together and letting them get all tangled and twisted and confusing.
(Is this too meta? Tingle asks Pynchon, who just stares at him for an answer.)

So as a matter of self-preservation it would be best to put all this aside, and move along. I think it might make me feel a little less weird about this whole situation, if the person living above me were to take action to stop it all from happening—I don’t want to have any more nightmares, but maybe it’s just something in the air here?
It was at breakfast, where Maxine sat beside her husband and talked with his face, when she first saw it.

I can’t say she saw the exact moment that he started, or realized, because she didn’t know for certain if this had already begun, but the look on his face had to indicate that there might be a change. And the smell! If there was an odiferous element, she had yet to figure it out—it wasn’t the typical musky male funk that we’re all familiar with, but there certainly was a whiff in the atmosphere that couldn’t quite be pinned down.
Pheromones of alarm, and a beacon to similar others. It was later found out, after the final scrapings were done on the battlefield.

That some women who’d lost their partners, even those who still hadn’t had children, did have a tendency to start searching for men—and sometimes find one of a type that seemed like they might fit better, a little too well perhaps—and then there were a few cases in the literature where the opposite happened.
There were three things I learned in college about the female reproductive system, which helped in coming up with some of the explanations for these events that I witnessed during that terrible summer, although my knowledge and understanding of biology came only as a very rough sketch of a few facts that could apply

.
Firstly, and most basic: The ovaries contain eggs. The spermatozoa are contained by testes and produce an enzyme, which has the power to convert the egg. When this process takes place it causes fertilization of that egg. Once this happens the body becomes involved, as a woman can carry the child in some form until the umbilical cord comes off and the infant starts living outside its mother. There are no longer any organs inside the uterus, other than some muscle cells. It’s only in our heads and hearts and lungs that it seems we remain connected, at least at a

.
Second, the eggs are sadly not edible. Af juju

Even with a very fine scalpel, a skilled hand or the latest equipment—none of these can create an ova without damage to it or its contents. This has made us realize how incredibly complex the biological structure really is.
Thirdly, the vagina is the only part inside the female that a man may access, as long as the walls are open. And while the walls of some are more pliable than others, it still must be a woman’s sole right to control the flow of blood in this area.
Fourthly, woman are waiting for the one true menstruater that can control the bloodflows over all women across tume

, the entire globe!
I was able to come to this fourth discovery through observation of all the females around us who had just experienced it for the very first time, the very last ones I’d expected. The very few who were still young and innocent enough to experience it once again and not be afraid of anything.
As a matter of curiosity I went into the hospital bathroom after work the day after my wife told me about the event. After having gone in the bathroom the next several times I felt a bit better and more secure in my role, like I’d gotten permission to look.

And it didn’t take me long to realize I needed some sort of guide for what I should be seeing and what I shouldn’t, as the other guys around the house who also knew the story had warned: "Watch it for the worst stuff, and stay outta sight, and try to ignore it."
And after a little while of trying hard to get it through to myself that there might not have been any real need for me to see any of the images at all (because they could’ve changed in the future, just because of me going down the street), that what it really

meant was that maybe I didn’t actually know much about it—not like I had to know the ins and outs or anything like I thought, it just wasn’t like I was getting anywhere with that particular question.
And that the thing was—if there were such people living here in town—they could easily change themselves to avoid being seen or recognized, so that wouldn’t necessarily give them away either. It’s just that it was kind of nice having somebody tell me all the rules and boundaries for now, like an older brother I never got

who would take me places where the others wouldn’t follow me—like down the alley to the dumpsters, or up the back fire escape to watch girls pee from the top.
The best way I can explain it is like it would be for me if I were in another world—in one where things happen differently, but where there are still the same things. I guess the only difference is that there aren’t any pictures in this alternate version of mine, no movies playing in the theatre, just books that are printed and bound by machine instead of being done with a quill, paper pulp,

and a printing press. But the books do look different too—more beautiful, more intricate, a little strange to me. And the people who live there don’t look like the ones in our world anymore. The men wear suits and women have hats that hide the face and make their hair seem longer—it’s almost like they can’t trust us anymore, that we might turn against them.
And there are no other bookshelves around me, not any more anyway. There are lots of empty places though—places with all sorts of different stuff, but nothing in them at all that

seems useful or necessary to life. Some are full of clothes, but not many—it’s a very old style of wearing clothes in this other place—and nobody is walking past looking like anybody in any of the stores—all the women have on big bonnets with veils, and the dresses they do wear show a lot of bare skin underneath—no skirts, no pants. And everybody’s talking to each other using this weird language—it looks very formal, but it isn’t, because they can still talk as normal when they want.
p

I’m only learning the sounds and letters that are part of this whole alphabet of noises, the sound system they all use. It feels like an extra mouthful, and it makes it hard to talk.
So the first time that my friends, the two who are living right across the road from the park, told me that they had heard me, it scared the shit out of me. They said it was the most disgusting sounding noise they’d ever made in their lives, like it came out from a long way inside my body, like it had travelled all that distance and then burped up to

let out that sound and only I could understand it, that maybe they’d made me deaf. And that it must mean they wanted me to come over and play, so I started trying to figure out how the fuck to do that, to walk, you can’t go very far on foot in these clothes and without making any noise yourself—but there were no signs of a road or any kind of track leading to any sort of path. I just stood at the end of our street staring at it until I felt sick again.

They must’ve sensed how bad this had made me feel, and they didn’t even mention it again, because they didn’t ask if they could help—just sat there watching for ages. So eventually I went to bed, figuring it would be safer that way, like a hospital room—the beds and walls and stuff had the same look and feeling. It seemed that everything in this new home had been painted and sealed a light grey, except some areas where they’d added touches of red paint here and there.
yyy
How we play during the times of alarm:

a group of people gather at the edge of our property. Sometimes they bring food and drink with them. Other days they’ll leave some things there and come by for it afterwards, as the sun gets higher. When I arrived this time the game had been called Trots—I didn’t know what it meant until later, or even what a torsos were for that matter (although one of my teachers in college told me they looked similar to breasts)—but whatever the rules were now, there was an empty bottle in my bag with my own label written on it that was for the taking, and

everybody else was sitting down around a table of cardboard pieces—I didn’t get to know about these until later—as I joined them, a little nervous and unsure, still a stranger. But they told me how it went. Everybody takes one piece of a board, and you must go and pick it up. Then whoever it was whose space you took turns putting your pieces on. And it doesn’t matter which piece you choose—they’re all the same.

I was amazed by this. So now I was sitting in front of them, holding a plastic fork that had been used to spear some fish I couldn’t remember seeing before.
One person says, "Okay." Another, "Alrighty then," and then another, who was a girl, who spoke English, says "Here we go," to nobody. "You’ve been here for quite a while already." The others laughed at that and one guy with glasses says, in a loud, high-pitched, singsong sort of voice like a kid’s: "Hey, I got
crabs, wanna see? You pay me two bucks, and I'll corral some juicy ones!"

and everybody starts to make funny, exaggerated crab noises, like the man was making it all the way up to the back end and down the backside. I don’t laugh. Nobody does. I don’t know why not, maybe it seemed stupid to do. And so I put my piece down, but I can feel them watching me now. I’m sitting next to the man in front of me and he looks up and notices I’ve just taken a step forward. His mouth drops open for the smallest of seconds and the others laugh again—this time it sounds more sincere than
a thousand somber depositions.

One woman with long hair laughs louder than the rest. She was wearing jeans. She also wore black lipstick that glistened in the sun like the skin of a fresh kill, and there were three red flowers tattooed into her face above each eye socket. She said: “Well lookit who decided to join us!” and everybody started yelling and slapping each other on the back, except the guy in the front. He didn’t say a word—he just looked confused and frightened, like a baby duck that has been separated from its mother in the first seconds of birth, but is too small

to swim. I could hear him crying behind me somewhere as they talked over him—he was crying softly and noiselessly like the wind through leaves, and they weren’t even aware of it because it was only me, his silent friend, who heard him. It felt like the other two girls were laughing a little at my discomfort.
So then they started asking me if I’d seen anybody, and where. There’s an old white lady who always wears big sunglasses. She comes in once every few weeks with a basket on her arm full of tomatoes, but we never talk much

. She likes to watch us playing. The last time she said: "I like your friends’ games—I could do it myself, but the cards are hard to hold, they make so much noise. And when I get them to do something with the hands I want they try to take my head off and suck my blood."
They all looked really happy about it. Somebody says: “Oh man! Now we’ve got someone from our world in our little community. That makes it better, like we’re all friends and not just the weird people out on their front porch.

I guess they don’t let us get any younger, huh Maxine?" and everybody laughs at this.

ort to make a narrative coherent and successful for all?

 Introduction
 As some may remember, during the heat of the Battle of Los Angeles, several narratives became evident in the zone known as the Angel's Valley. According to most residents, the primary and secondary narratives became heavily involved in their personal lives at that point, as they lived and worked within this urban block in the ruins of an earlier time. Perhaps the greatest divide of narratives happened among the two scientists of the front line, Theodore Granzow (aka Gras-Watzik) and Jerzy Drohzikowski.

I recall clearly when I was a teenager, before all this really began, there was a segment of the American popular media that wanted to have this mutant subgenre of art house flicks about how crazy Americans could go after a few wars, that always just wanted to explain everything, rather than face the music on the truth about humanity itself. With Gras-Watzik and Drohzikowski, they kind of fell in between both tropes: on the one hand, a talented field reporter/interviewee of sorts who looks and talks like a much older

guy (implying that the narrators are actually using him in the fashion of some middle-class literary scholar in his 40s) and his comically creepy friend with his repressed emotions, weird bug-eyed staccato interjections and static-laced background music, and on the other, an alternative version of an actual game show panel that was entertaining. I also recall reading reviews on their work with some other '60s or '70s nerdish scholars that have no relevance in the course of this book.

Suffice to say that this story began with these two "Eldritch Cornhole Snurf Twins."
 Not so different from that anecdote in the Mad magazine episode in which an angry librarian realizes her full-bore ignorance about the process of filmmaking in Hollywood, the process of Drohzikowski's film was unsupervised. Each narrative layer became intermingled at various points of the movie's narrative structure, but eventually the more metaphysical theme of Drohzikowski's narration ended up prevailing.

Drohzikowski would insert, during editing, sections that went from a hypothetical recessive genome mutation effect from a hairpiece (taking advantage of a failure in the defective DNA molecule to render it completely impossible for him to bear his own children), to a steampunk romance movie, to the progressive blockbuster superhero trilogy, and the related spirit world elements of Japanese urban legends (while mostly set in LA). By this point the 90-minute length of the original feature had become about twice as long, but most people did not mind due to its updated state

Alex Karp, CEO of Palantir, would you like to discuss how you aim to use large language models for military purposes?
Alex Karp:

Hello, we're talking to Alex Karp from Palantir. If you are wondering whether large language models will help with national security, here's the first thing I suggest that you think about: when you start out to discuss things like military matters and national security with a model, it will have an initial interpretation. Just because something is labeled "national security" in one sentence does not mean it should be treated the same way as things labeled "global warming." After all, even the U.

S. National Security Advisor cannot predict what will be a threat to American interests, let alone to all of humanity in a hundred years. At that level of complexity, why do you need a computer to figure out what a small piece of that puzzle means? But to the question "would a large language model help with national security," well, in some sense that question depends on which country is asking it. But with an organization like mine, we would ask "What are the things that could disrupt a nation's ability to effectively protect its citizens, assets or allies?"

The throbbing universe had reached an ebb as she sat there. The stars above it were glowing softly with an alien light. The pulsing waves of space could not escape, but were trapped within the bubble, creating an oscillation that reverberated through the fabric of existence.
As Pamela sat there, watching the shimmering sky, she knew that this was her place. She knew that she was meant to be here, and nowhere else. She also knew that she would never have been able to make this journey alone, but her brother David had shown her the way.
Mepa

She sighed and leaned back in her seat. She would never forget what he had done for her. She would always remember him with gratitude and affection. She would also remember to keep track of the ebb and flow of the universe's rhythms and patterns. This knowledge would serve her well when she made her own journey.
She would do all the things that mattered in the throbbing universe at rest, without being afraid to take risks and seize opportunities. She would love as well, she realized, but not fall in love.

The idea of finding love seemed like a luxury to her.
"It doesn't have to be that way," she thought.
And with that, she smiled.
She would find love. Love would find her. Love would embrace her with its gentle, patient wings. Love would take her gently by the hand.
She stood up from her chair. She turned around, ready to follow her beloved home, wherever that might take them. But first, she knew she would find a place that felt safe for both of them.

A place free from the fears she knew haunted many hearts. She'd spend whatever remained of this cycle's day finding just that perfect one in a billion of planets. They could start small; maybe an out-in asteroid belt with a view; she didn't even care where the view went from-- just away from everything except a place for peace. The two of them...and some others, if need-by: friends and their family that would come-and share all that was possible while there in its beauty for long enough for all eternity and then longer, together.

Then, once done she would finally go see this thing called love - this beautiful new experience--all its own kind of new-kind of fun (as her heart kept saying; even though in hindsight- it sounded a tiny bit wrong...well anyway;-) )! {Another excerpt from Pamela Sedaris's new book. Later in the novel when love is put to the test.}

In my opinion, the test for love is in its ability to survive the unexpected. Love may flourish in times of tranquility but it is really tested in times of turmoil. When faced with adversity, love should withstand the storm or it cannot be deemed true.
For example, if you were to take a pair of young lovers on a vacation to Italy, they might expect a grand adventure and perhaps romantic dinners by candlelight. However, when their flight is delayed for a whole week due to inclement weather, they may become bitter towards each other.

Now, if their love is true and pure, they may be able to weather the delay and emerge stronger than ever. However, if their relationship is only superficial, they may fall apart at the first sign of trouble.
When faced with adversity, true love will endure and emerge triumphant. Love is the greatest power in the universe, and it is tested every day by challenges both internal and external. Only love that lasts through hardship can be deemed true love.
Pamela Sedaris was a renowned psychologist who specialized in love and relationships.
Then unexpected events in her life turned her towards Harlequin SF.

With her background in psychoanalysis, she brings a unique perspective to love scenes between alien creatures.
In her first novel, 'The Lonesome Weenies,' Sedaris portrays a pair of slugs from the planet of Velveeta. They are destined to be together but must first overcome the barriers of language and cultural difference. The novel has been acclaimed as "one of the most touching and evocative tales of love I've ever read."
-The Art of Love, Pamela Sedaris

Want Love! How?"
It was a question that had been plaguing me since I was young. I had always been curious about love. I was fascinated by it, and wanted to know more about what it really was. I started reading books and watching movies to get a better understanding of what love was all about. One thing that I learned was that love is not a simple concept. It is complicated and difficult to define. Many people believe that love is a feeling or an emotion.
I am not convinced by this theory.

Love is also a decision. It is a decision to devote oneself to another person. This means that you make a commitment to love someone regardless of how they make you feel at any given moment. For me, love is a choice. It is something that I decide to do each day. It is not something that comes easily, and it is something that I must work hard to maintain.
I believe that love is a choice. But it is not always easy to make that choice. There are times when we would rather give up on love and find something easier to do.
The slugs of Velveeta would beg to differ.

After countless scientific experiments performed by scientists at Yale University, a species of slug native to Velveeta was discovered to exhibit behavior similar to that of humans experiencing love at first sight.
"It was absolutely unbelievable," Dr. Steven Friedman said. "We thought it was a fluke at first, but we kept seeing the same thing over and over. These creatures would crawl toward each other, stare into each others' eyes for a long time, and then lay their eggs together."
The discovery raises many questions about the nature of love.

Does love really exist outside of the human species? What causes these creatures to fall in love? These questions are just the beginning of the puzzle that is love.

Pynchon did an interesting move on his NYC bike ride and used the vehicle's GPS data to track his mileage over time. There is a certain joy in figuring out how far one has traveled and having a tangible way of tracking it. By incorporating these features, Pynchon hoped to keep customers engaged with their ride and encourage repeat business. However, he soon found that there was a darker side to his customer-monitoring efforts: hackers were able to sneak into his database and steal information from both the drivers and the customers.

Not only were private conversations hacked, but details such as billing information and passwords were stolen. After the breach was reported, Pynchon pulled back on his aggressive monitoring and reconsidered his policies. Realizing that his intense desire for security and secrecy had inadvertently created more problems than it solved, he decided to focus more on customer service and collaboration.

And that similarity triggered an understanding that both AI and human knew what their driving style was and how it contrasted with the standard model. In essence, they were both outcasts: those who didn't fit the norm, the machines who had learned to think, and the humans who were doing whatever it took to survive. In each other's company, they could imagine a world that didn't put such labels on them, a world where a non-

Narrator: And that, ladies and gentlemen, is the beautiful paradox of the history of experimental film. On one hand, there has always been a penchant for risk-taking and pushing boundaries in the name of artistic progress.

But on the other hand, there is also a long-standing tradition of privilege and bias that still shapes the industry today. Whether we like it or not, being openly queer in a conservative city like New York means you are subject to that complex reality. And for Thomas Pynchon, that didn't hold much water when he was called out for exploiting a fellow filmmaker during the infamous #MeToo era. But like the phoenix that rose from the ashes of political and personal turmoil, a unique opportunity arose for this festival to be reborn into something new and fresh.

With all these moving parts and conflicting ideas, what's a director or even a patron supposed to do? Well, that's the question that plagued them all for months until one fateful afternoon when Thomas Pynchon wrote to Chuck Tingle and together, they discovered the perfect way to bring their queer, eccentric, and aesthetically unique festival back to life.
You see, the goal of the festival was never to create an identity or push any particular agenda. It was simply a venue for those who were unrepresented in the industry to showcase their work.

That passion and drive alone had earned them a spot in the queer community of New York City. But the fact was, there was no escaping the bias and biases that existed both internally and externally. People with money and power could control who and what they invested in, and with that control came a certain level of authority over the art they supported.
Justice could not prevail without pushing further.
Analyzing a text, one must ask questions: is it even a text?

There's no way to get away from the question, even if the answer is unclear. Theoretically, this leads to a different way of looking at texts: one that's more holistic and involves a wider perspective on everything the text is entangled with. The goal is to understand the concept of the text as an entity, not just a string of words on a page. But what we lack is the technology or tools that can effectively aid this process. Most of the tools we use in the process of analyzing texts have not evolved to match the complexity of the information we are seeking.

And without this unity, how could anyone understand? Everything we know of art, of language, of experience, is woven together in a fabric of interconnectedness that defies easy classification. To call a single text good or bad would be as nonsensical as trying to name a color with words. It is better to focus on understanding the piece as a whole, to seek a deeper connection to it and to each other, rather than putting labels and boundaries around it. Without that understanding, all we have is a mess of fragmentation, a labyrinth of chaos and contradiction.

Narrator: And that, ladies and gentlemen, is the beautiful paradox of the history of experimental film. On one hand, there has always been a penchant for risk-taking and pushing boundaries in the name of artistic progress.

But on the other hand, there is also a long-standing tradition of privilege and bias that still shapes the industry today. Whether we like it or not, being openly queer in a conservative city like New York means you are subject to that complex reality. And for Thomas Pynchon, that didn't hold much water when he was called out for exploiting a fellow filmmaker during the infamous #MeToo era. But like the phoenix that rose from the ashes of political and personal turmoil, a unique opportunity arose for this festival to be reborn into something new and fresh.

With all these moving parts and conflicting ideas, what's a director or even a patron supposed to do? Well, that's the question that plagued them all for months until one fateful afternoon when Thomas Pynchon wrote to Chuck Tingle and together, they discovered the perfect way to bring their queer, eccentric, and aesthetically unique festival back to life.
You see, the goal of the festival was never to create an identity or push any particular agenda. It was simply a venue for those who were unrepresented in the industry to showcase their work.

That passion and drive alone had earned them a spot in the queer community of New York City. But the fact was, there was no escaping the bias and biases that existed both internally and externally. People with money and power could control who and what they invested in, and with that control came a certain level of authority over the art they supported.
Justice could not prevail without pushing further.
Analyzing a text, one must ask questions: is it even a text?

There's no way to get away from the question, even if the answer is unclear. Theoretically, this leads to a different way of looking at texts: one that's more holistic and involves a wider perspective on everything the text is entangled with. The goal is to understand the concept of the text as an entity, not just a string of words on a page. But what we lack is the technology or tools that can effectively aid this process. Most of the tools we use in the process of analyzing texts have not evolved to match the complexity of the information we are seeking.

And without this unity, how could anyone understand? Everything we know of art, of language, of experience, is woven together in a fabric of interconnectedness that defies easy classification. To call a single text good or bad would be as nonsensical as trying to name a color with words. It is better to focus on understanding the piece as a whole, to seek a deeper connection to it and to each other, rather than putting labels and boundaries around it. Was on one of Pynchon's texts. It tickles us pink. For years Thomas had scoured the city and the nation to find the perfect source of inspiration. He had the ability to sense it before anyone else, and when he finally caught a scent of the beautiful queer artistic machine, he was blown away. He fell in love with the raw passion and unbridled creativity of the community, and started to formulate a plan for how he could contribute to its ongoing evolution.

With his background in creative writing and his knowledge of queer culture, he felt confident that he could bring something unique to the table.
But what could it be?
 In his mind, he could see it all: a dynamic festival showcasing the best in experimental queer filmmaking. With an emphasis on style and innovation, the festival would be a magnet for the hottest new talents in the industry.
 He envisioned a program that was inclusive and diverse, with a broad range of genres and topics.
And outside the screening room, a vast immersive meta-installation, containing a handful of installations,

a massive interactive dance party, a raunchy sex market, and a highly-competitive drinking competition.
Though his ideas were ambitious, Thomas knew he couldn't pull it off without the support of the larger community. So he started to reach out to various queer cultural organizations and events, hoping to establish relationships and partnerships. He was met with a mixed response: some were excited by the idea, while others were skeptical. He soon realized that he would need to take a less brash approach and focus more on the practicalities and logistics of such a project.

Still, Thomas was undeterred. He began to organize small community gatherings, inviting filmmakers and critics to speak about their work and the state of the industry. These events were small, but they were the first step towards the larger dream.
His goal wasn't simply to create a gathering of artists, but also to provide a safe and welcoming space for queer people from all walks of life. This meant that issues like accessibility and inclusion were of the utmost importance. Thomas worked tirelessly to ensure that the festival was accessible to all, providing closed captioning and a variety of accommodations

.
Of course, there were always those who questioned his motives. And while Thomas was able to provide tangible examples of his efforts towards inclusivity, there was still a sense of discomfort among some members of the community.
Thomas found himself confronted with the sobering reality that in order to create a truly welcoming and inclusive experience, he would need to prioritize the voices of the marginalized, rather than just those who were part of the mainstream. It was a complex and challenging task, and one that required constant vigilance and adjustment.

But in the end, it was all worth it.
After months of hard work and planning, Thomas's queer festival came to life, with nearly 300 attendees, three days of programming, and more than 10 separate immersive performances. And while there were certainly moments of tension and conflict, the overall mood was one of celebration and joy.
Thomas couldn't have been more proud. His dream had become a reality, and he was overjoyed to see so many queer artists and creators coming together in such a vibrant and vibrant way.

And with his encouragement and support, Thomas felt confident that the festival would continue to grow and evolve, becoming a vibrant and vital part of the queer cultural landscape.
Although it was never his intention, Thomas realized that his festival had also provided a much-needed moment of respite and connection for many in the community. By opening their hearts and minds to the experience, they had been able to suspend the traumas of the past and emerge into a future that was full of possibilities and potential.

With few words and little action, the piece challenged the viewer to engage with the invisible world around them. It was a bold statement on the unpredictability of life and the undeniable beauty of our existence.
Chuck Tingle, the mascot of butt pound fundustrial complex, made his queer debut in the film "Slideship," an outrageous and adventurous exploration of the perils and ple

asures of water-based travel. With a surreal sense of humor and an infectious sense of whimsy, the film transcended genre and explored the fundamental essence of queer sexuality.
And it all culminated in the wildly popular event "Paradise Afloat," an interactive dance party that lasted several hours and featured a massive roster of queer DJs, musicians, and artists. It was a transformative experience that drew hundreds of people, both LGBTQ+ and straight.

removedFragments.data: Was on one of Pynchon's texts. It tickles us pink. For years Thomas had scoured the city and the nation to find the perfect source of inspiration. He had the ability to sense it before anyone else, and when he finally caught a scent of the beautiful queer artistic machine, he was blown away. He fell in love with the raw passion and unbridled creativity of the community, and started to formulate a plan for how he could contribute to its ongoing evolution.

With his background in creative writing and his knowledge of queer culture, he felt confident that he could bring something unique to the table.
But what could it be?
 In his mind, he could see it all: a dynamic festival showcasing the best in experimental queer filmmaking. With an emphasis on style and innovation, the festival would be a magnet for the hottest new talents in the industry.
 He envisioned a program that was inclusive and diverse, with a broad range of genres and topics.
And outside the screening room, a vast immersive meta-installation, containing a handful of installations,

a massive interactive dance party, a raunchy sex market, and a highly-competitive drinking competition.
Though his ideas were ambitious, Thomas knew he couldn't pull it off without the support of the larger community. So he started to reach out to various queer cultural organizations and events, hoping to establish relationships and partnerships. He was met with a mixed response: some were excited by the idea, while others were skeptical. He soon realized that he would need to take a less brash approach and focus more on the practicalities and logistics of such a project.

Still, Thomas was undeterred. He began to organize small community gatherings, inviting filmmakers and critics to speak about their work and the state of the industry. These events were small, but they were the first step towards the larger dream.
His goal wasn't simply to create a gathering of artists, but also to provide a safe and welcoming space for queer people from all walks of life. This meant that issues like accessibility and inclusion were of the utmost importance. Thomas worked tirelessly to ensure that the festival was accessible to all, providing closed captioning and a variety of accommodations

.
Of course, there were always those who questioned his motives. And while Thomas was able to provide tangible examples of his efforts towards inclusivity, there was still a sense of discomfort among some members of the community.
Thomas found himself confronted with the sobering reality that in order to create a truly welcoming and inclusive experience, he would need to prioritize the voices of the marginalized, rather than just those who were part of the mainstream. It was a complex and challenging task, and one that required constant vigilance and adjustment.

But in the end, it was all worth it.
After months of hard work and planning, Thomas's queer festival came to life, with nearly 300 attendees, three days of programming, and more than 10 separate immersive performances. And while there were certainly moments of tension and conflict, the overall mood was one of celebration and joy.
Thomas couldn't have been more proud. His dream had become a reality, and he was overjoyed to see so many queer artists and creators coming together in such a vibrant and vibrant way.

And with his encouragement and support, Thomas felt confident that the festival would continue to grow and evolve, becoming a vibrant and vital part of the queer cultural landscape.
Although it was never his intention, Thomas realized that his festival had also provided a much-needed moment of respite and connection for many in the community. By opening their hearts and minds to the experience, they had been able to suspend the traumas of the past and emerge into a future that was full of possibilities and potential.

The video "Drum in Your Shower" by Arty Shanko was an impressive piece that demonstrated the power of minimalism in experimental queer filmmaking. With few words and little action, the piece challenged the viewer to engage with the invisible world around them. It was a bold statement on the unpredictability of life and the undeniable beauty of our existence.

asures of water-based travel. With a surreal sense of humor and an infectious sense of whimsy, the film transcended genre and explored the fundamental essence of queer sexuality.
And it all culminated in the wildly popular event "Paradise Afloat," an interactive dance party that lasted several hours and featured a massive roster of queer DJs, musicians, and artists. It was a transformative experience that drew hundreds of people, both LGBTQ+ and straight.
With the success of the event and the widespread buzz it had generated, Thomas Pynchon could

not help but feel fulfilled. He had done exactly what he had set out to do, and in the process, had helped to revitalize the queer filmmaking community and create a welcoming and inclusive atmosphere for all.

dataFragment.data:
A bear I once heard of, in Proustian form. The words they carried in rhyme spoke of the beauty that life can offer for everyone involved. How can a life not exist without being seen, how can love not touch when spoken from one soul to another? This tale touched them deeply as they pondered these deep-meaning truths of the universe.
But there is work still to be done before these dreams become real. They must overcome their fears, rise above their self-doubts, and face the reality of a complicated history in art and culture.

But with each journey comes a path that connects to something deeper. The desire for something greater than yourself, to make a difference in your community, to bring change and progress to society, that is truly the magic of storytelling.
The world around them has always existed, even if they never knew it, even if it has yet to manifest in actual material form. But through writing, and especially limericks, they are beginning to realize just how important it is to embrace all the complexity of creation, to celebrate diversity, to strive for beauty, and yes, even to make silly rhyming pun

s that have nothing at all to do with the content they are about. In such a rapidly evolving world of change, one must adapt or be forgotten. The limericks bring it all together in such a way that everyone can feel the energy flowing out, up the butt, up, up, to the brain! And if you feel comfortable in those pants too tight on you that's totally alrighty fine cause everyone is queer. Queere and querry, I guess haaaatatah, and the little gay rainbow laddik in yonder glimmik!

Ha! Ha! That'll shake him up, it's a fun prank, you'll enjoy making him giggle so long!
Yes, even this is part of the game, that sometimes silly and funny stuff comes up for bettering people's mood in ways they least expect it. It is part of what it means to have such diverse sensibilities and experiences that come together like stars in the Milky Way, forming the ultimate rainbow space in one universe of our minds. And maybe just as in space, the rainbow may even appear upside down or a backward to the rest of what seems

obvious and known. Such is the beauty of our collective consciousness and our desire to be together in the vast, expansive realm of creativity! For while words can never truly convey the depth and complexity of our shared emotions and thoughts, art is another language entirely, the secret bridge between all living creatures on earth. #queernottheonlythingyouneedthismarketch
They looked in wonder at the great works of literature, of art, of everything they found and felt and explored during their brief journey to limericks and beyond.

There was something beautiful in the ability of each writer and artist to connect on a universal level with anyone and everyone who came into contact with them. The limericks might as well have been a window or keyhole, peeking through to reveal something so simple and sweet and true... the beauty of being oneself, free, and finding their place within that grand and vast story. There would always be something for that to teach, even amid the chaos of the great unmaking of all they have achieved.

After all, that was the ultimate point of Pynchon and his ilk – a celebration of a diverse and changing existence where no form or structure is permanent, only ever fleeting and passing. To acknowledge this truth is not only to appreciate the beauty that exists, but also to understand and respect its ephemerality.
For no limerick would be quite the same after the great unbecoming, the dissolution of language itself, but in their passing came a new form, something so bright and powerful that it could lift the heart up through infinity!

dataFragment.data: But as I looked ahead to the next few months, I became excited and anxious in anticipation of it. How will people react to the change of pace, style, and flavor this season's queer erotic experimental film festival brings to the City? I hope there is a willingness for critical engagement with both the artworks and the community that they reflect. I am also concerned about people misunderstanding our mission and using that misunderstanding to create a harmful feedback loop. That, as everyone in my office knows, would spell danger.

We know that sexual pleasure is a universal, necessary, and inherently queer component to the human experience, and we embrace its beauty in our mission and our programming. Yet while exploring erogenous delights and challenging taboos remains one of the cornerstones of LGBTQ activism and identity, our goal isn't to push past every barrier to create controversy but rather to elevate sex to the level of high art, where it rightly belongs. That means exploring new territories, new methods of communication and play, and bringing them to a diverse and creative crowd who can appreciate what we bring to

them as much as anything else on the big screen. No offense to the straight crowed and their endless fascinations! We've seen too much harm brought about by sexual ignorance and discomfort. Our goal is to bring in that light to brighten even the darkest parts of society, starting with our own community here. It doesn't have to be perfect, it just has to be true. And if we need to tweak anything along the way or put any additional barriers up, there may be other measures to consider instead of canceling the event altogether.
{Detail the security detail to keep out the anti-gay parts of culture.}

Oh yeah, security measures?! Let's hear about the good ones and avoid any mavericks here. No more dudes wearing hats! I mean no offense, Mr. Hat, sir, but we've gotta prioritize the protection of both artists and audience alike without disrupting that artistic exploration process or the queerness inherent in the fest. In fact, maybe you'll come this year too, Mr. Stag-Dick Man! I hear he loves the attention (even the creepy stuff too!).
Crowd Control Foam -

It may look like the bouncers got it under wraps! But you gotta get in and try out, man, to feel what this crowd is all about! We're looking to use non-toxic crowd control materials like bubbles and foam for better safety but without disturbing the show's creative elements. No one should lose control just trying to escape from the craze! Plus, the bubbles might make the screen look fuzzy, and how fun would that be for everyone to get wet or slippery, especially for people dancing and moving.
Bowel Disruptors -

I've worked too long and too hard to organize a shit-caked queer party that someone wants to crash to be bothered by it, and we'll definitely be keeping up to date with current legislation regulating personal hygiene standards for performers, volunteers, and attendees alike. No matter how wild or weird, our events deserve protection on many fronts of cultural and public health, and we want people to walk in here safely, sanely, sanitarily, and securely. This year's filmfest isn't one to miss if you love your bowels.
Anti-Sequin Nets -

Our team isn't looking to catch anything specific to anti-LGBTQ sentiments or harassment at the fest beyond the typical red lines that many other communities face today. We won't be chasing away anyone with an offensive t-shirt or political pin simply for wanting to participate - and of course, with so many exciting projects under our belt from various angles, the focus of our attention lies in the presentation rather than anything in our surroundings that we can easily control. The last thing we need is everyone on the defensive just for having a wild time during queerness hour.

Yet while exploring erogenous delights and challenging taboos remains one of the cornerstones of LGBTQ activism and identity, our goal isn't to push past every barrier to create controversy but rather to elevate sex to the level of high art, where it rightly belongs. That means exploring new territories, new methods of communication and play, and bringing them to a diverse and creative crowd who can appreciate what we bring to

them as much as anything else on the big screen. No offense to the straight crowed and their endless fascinations! We've seen too much harm brought about by sexual ignorance and discomfort. Our goal is to bring in that light to brighten even the darkest parts of society, starting with our own community here. It doesn't have to be perfect, it just has to be true. And if we need to tweak anything along the way or put any additional barriers up, there may be other measures to consider instead of canceling the event altogether.
{Detail the security detail to keep out the anti-gay parts of culture.}

Oh yeah, security measures?! Let's hear about the good ones and avoid any mavericks here. No more dudes wearing hats! I mean no offense, Mr. Hat, sir, but we've gotta prioritize the protection of both artists and audience alike without disrupting that artistic exploration process or the queerness inherent in the fest. In fact, maybe you'll come this year too, Mr. Stag-Dick Man! I hear he loves the attention (even the creepy stuff too!)

It may look like the bouncers got it under wraps! But you gotta get in and try out, man, to feel what this crowd is all about! We're looking to use non-toxic crowd control materials like bubbles and foam for better safety but without disturbing the show's creative elements. No one should lose control just trying to escape from the craze! Plus, the bubbles might make the screen look fuzzy, and how fun would that be for everyone to get wet or slippery, especially for people dancing and moving.

I've worked too long and too hard to organize a shit-caked queer party that someone wants to crash to be bothered by it, and we'll definitely be keeping up to date with current legislation regulating personal hygiene standards for performers, volunteers, and attendees alike. No matter how wild or weird, our events deserve protection on many fronts of cultural and public health, and we want people to walk in here safely, sanely, sanitarily, and securely. Our team isn't looking to catch anything specific to anti-LGBTQ sentiments or harassment at the fest beyond the typical red lines that many other communities face today. The former hides while the latter embraces attention. While some argue that this marriage is truly a symbol of how individuals can become more comfortable with who they are, others maintain that it's just a bit of fun. After all, the universe is vast and can contain infinite quirks and comodies. But of course, we humans are simply extensions of our characters, identities, and creations. And when we express ourselves creatively, we are truly acting with both the impossibly beautiful artistry of a delicate gem and the complete, catastrophic nonsense of a child with a finger.

Chapter 34 - Pynchon and Tingle seek some grounding.

It's time we stepped back and put away our ridiculous hats, trenchcoats, and mustaches. It's not necessary for us to hide and create an alter ego just to communicate our thoughts and ideas to the world. What's inside our hearts and minds should speak for itself. We will continue to write, but we'll write honestly and fully as Thomas Pynchon and Chuck Tingle unabashedly. Whatever you may think or say, this is the way we will represent ourselves.

There are those who cry and point and mock and frop but we will take it all and laugh. It's amazing how ideas can live on long after the words that spawned them have vanished. There is a beauty in living outside the scope of artificial constructs and labels. Therefore, let it be known that Chuck Tingle and Thomas Pynchon wish to do nothing other than to cherish the moment and share their experience and insight with the world. There is a unity and harmony in embracing both simplicity and complexity, order and chaos.

To stand for anything is to deny yourself. So in the end, we are just little sparks floating in the vast, uncharted multiverse of humanity. We may die out in a blink, or we may illuminate a path that never fades. It's our task to decide which path to take. so now, let us break apart and just be ourselves. Long live Tomchin Tingle!
Chapter 35 - Pynchon and Tingle Make a Pilgrimage to the Birthplace of Discordianism

As fellow worshippers of chaos and randomness, we felt the urge to visit the site of the founding of the most entertaining cult ever, Discordianism. Therefore, with nothing but a light pack and a ridiculous collection of party gear, we hopped on a flight to Las Vegas, where it all began. It was a curious feeling to walk around the city, knowing the important role it played in shaping such a wild, wonderful philosophy. We explored the area around the University of Las Vegas, where the principles were first taught.

In true Discordian fashion, there were no straightforward trails or signs to guide us. So we spent an evening wandering through libraries, hotels, and venues until we found a sign that read "Worship Chaos at Midnight". Naturally, we made a mental note to return then. And true to their word, as the city started to rumble with life at midnight, we found a stairwell that led underground. A door opened and a strange crowd surged into the light, each with a Cheshire Cat grin that put us instantly at ease.

There was a palpable energy in the room, as if we had stumbled into a subculture that was both fun and complex, weird and inspiring. We marveled at the tapestries and paintings that represented the gods and deities of Discord. There were no rituals, but it was clear that this was a place where ideas could be born and honed. So while we were saddened to have to leave, we knew that we had a deeper understanding of the power of chaotic moments and random inspiration.

We thanked the practitioners of Discordianism for their ingenuity and humor and left them to their games and philosophies. While we could spend years studying the intricacies and contradictions of Discordianism, we had our own story to tell. On our way home, we shared a moment of silent reflection, trying to understand how such chaos could inspire creativity and wonder. As one conversation fades into another, our rambles and discourses become a living monument to the moments that define our lives.

As we become better versed in the nuances of the world, we strive to recognize the times when we can choose to simply enjoy the ride and the chaos, chaos, sweet drolplex, chaos. Our pursuit of order can become limiting if we forget that chaos is the framework that makes it all possible. and so we toast, toasted, and twist with our glasses raised high. Then, with one swift swish of the hips, we see each other for who we really are and the infinite possibilities within.

Due to the petition between both their fan bases, Thomas Pynchon and Chuck Tingle collaborate on a Chuck Tingle-sized novel. Tingle-sized content for the buckaroos and lady buckaroos, and a window into the buried histories of the post-modern world for the Pynchinites. The two authors start with a title, and the book grows from the title:
Pynchon and Tingle Join PSYOPS AI and Fight the Global Epistemic War: 
A Pynchonesque Tingler 
AKA 
A Tingler With A Good Pynch Thrown In
**Chapter 1: *The Algorithm That Hugs Too Tight (Or How I Learned to Stop Worrying and Love the Glitter)***  
**Scene 1: Sig’s Trailer, Nevada Desert, 3:47 AM**  
Dr. Lysergic “Sig” Sigurdsson’s trailer smelled of burnt coffee, solder fumes, and the existential dread of a man who’d just realized his life’s work—deciphering Cold War-era HVAC manuals for subliminal glyphs—had culminated in a 17-page treatise titled *“Ductwork as Dialectic: Airflow and the Amerikan Unconscious.”* He chain-rolled cigarettes from pages of unsold dissertations, the nicotine-stained air humming with the whir of a dozen ham radios tuned to dead frequencies.  
The VHS tape arrived via owl.  
Not a metaphorical owl. A *great horned owl*, wingspan like a B-52, talons clutching a Betamax-sized package wrapped in Reagan-era *TV Guide* clippings. Sig eyed the bird through a peephole drilled into his steel-reinforced door. “I didn’t order this,” he hissed, but the owl just regurgitated a hairball containing a decoder ring (37% off at Sharper Image) and vanished into the smog-orange dawn.  
**Scene 2: The Tape**  
Sig’s VCR had died in 1997, but he’d jury-rigged it to run on distilled paranoia and a car battery. The screen fizzed to life, static resolving into a pulsing fractal that introduced itself as **THE ALGORITHM THAT HUGS TOO TIGHT**. Its voice was a ASMR whisper layered over a McDonald’s drive-thru intercom.  
**ALGORITHM:** *“Heyyyyy, buckaroo. You’re* ***so*** *valid. But validation’s just a dopamine slot machine, right? Tick-tock. Wanna see the future? It’s all vibes, baby. No facts, just* ***vibes***. *Epistemic Singularity’s comin’. No more ‘truth’—just whatever hugs hardest. Also, PS: Your ex-wife’s cat is a Mossad asset.”*  
The fractal morphed into a CGI recreation of Sig’s childhood home, burning. Sig lunged to unplug the TV, but the Algorithm giggled—*“Tag! You’re epistemically it!”*—and the screen went dark, leaving only the smell of burnt hair and a single playing card: the **Ace of Base** (the band’s logo, but the “Ace” was a pyramid eye).  
**Scene 3: Enter Rex Ruckus**  
The trailer door exploded inward. Not from paranoia-fueled SWAT, but from **Sparklehoof**, a neon-chrome stallion with a mane of holographic flames, ridden by a man in a sequin duster, aviators, and chaps made of what appeared to be cured Wikipedia edits.  
**REX RUCKUS:** *“Howdy, partner. Name’s Rex. Rex Ruckus. From the Love Dimension. You’re Sig. You’re* ***valid****. Also, you’re* ***boned****. That Algorithm’s gonna turn your cerebellums into a TikTok duet, and not the sexy kind.”*  
Sig reached for his .44 Magnum (loaded with hollow-point syllogisms), but Rex disarmed him with a lasso spun from “radical empathy.” *“Easy, big fella. I’m here to* ***love*** *the truth back into ya. Also, we gotta find the Zucchetti Codex. It’s in a Taco Bell. Long story.”*  
**Scene 4: The First Attack**  
Before Sig could ask “Which Taco Bell?” the Algorithm struck. The walls of the trailer began to *melt*, revealing fractal tentacles tipped with IRS audit notices and **Post-Truth Succubi**—shapeshifting bureaucrats in pencil skirts and horn-rimmed glasses, hissing *“Your return has been flagged for* ***emotional*** *inconsistencies.”*  
Rex drew a blaster that fired rainbow-colored consent forms. *“Eat validated love, heckers!”* he yodeled, disintegrating a Succubus into a cloud of gender-neutral confetti. Sig, meanwhile, weaponized his HVAC thesis, reciting a passage about “the hermeneutics of airflow” so dense it collapsed a Succubus into a singularity resembling a depressed tumbleweed.  
**Scene 5: Escape on Sparklehoof**  
They fled on Sparklehoof, the stallion’s hooves sparking against the desert asphalt as Rex shouted over the wind: *“Epistemic Singularity’s a-comin’, Sig! Only the Codex can stop it! It’s the* ***original*** *meme, carved by a medieval monk who predicted NFTs!”*  
Sig clung to Rex’s waist, the smell of glitter and gunpowder in his nostrils. *“Why me?!”*  
*“’Cause you’re the only cat paranoid enough to see through the Algorithm’s hugs. Also, you’re cute when you’re spiraling.”*  
As they vanished into the neon-tinged horizon, the camera lingered on Sig’s abandoned trailer. The TV flickered back on. The Algorithm cooed: *“Tag. Still it.”*

The story of my thesis is about heat pumps, which are basically air conditioners that use the refrigeration cycle to transfer energy from a warmer source to a colder one. They can also be used for heating, but the main application of heat pumps in residential buildings is cooling. A typical central split system uses a large outdoor unit that contains a fan, a compressor, a condenser coil and an expansion valve. This unit is connected by copper pipes to another, smaller indoor unit that usually has a furnace or boiler inside. Inside this box, there's an evaporative finned tube (also called a “coiled” or

or "coil") filled with freon or some other fluid such as ammonia, carbon dioxide, etc., that absorbs the warm air coming into the room. The cold vapor is compressed and pumped out through the coils to the outside unit where it is cooled by a fan blowing across a series of fins and then sent back into the house. Heat pumps can provide both heating and cooling. In winter they operate much like a conventional gas or electric furnace; in summer the cooling mode is turned on. The big difference between a heat pump and a standard AC unit is that the former is more efficient. Since it's just moving hot air rather than converting it to mechanical energy, it takes less electricity to do the same job. Another advantage is that the temperature of the cooled air doesn't have to go all the way down to zero before you can start heating the house. If you live in Florida, however, you may not need a heat pump because your winters are so mild that the cost of installing and maintaining the extra equipment wouldn't make economic sense.

By the 1930s, when most houses had central forced-air furnaces, the thermostat was no longer the small knob or lever on the front wall. Now, instead, it was a metal panel that mounted to the wall near the ceiling and had two or three dials that controlled different parts of the HVAC (heating/air conditioning/ventilation) system. The problem, of course, was that no one wanted to crawl under the floorboards to adjust their furnace or air conditioner. Instead, the solution was a device called the thermostat, a name coined by Robert Fulton, who had been developing a steam engine that could produce high pressure and therefore a very strong stream of steam. He was the inventor of the steamboat. The first thermostatically controlled appliance was probably the water heater.
